summary: Follow-up of the accepted T.3 part for T.5, tame kernels and explicit arithmetic. Every T.5 target is already a node of that part: the unramified subgroup, the tame-kernel sequences of O_F and O_{F,S} and the relative sequence, the real sign symbol, K₂(ℤ) ≅ ℤ/2 and K₂(ℚ). K₂(𝔽_q) = 0 is T.2/k2-finite-field. The one open input was Steinberg's theorem that the monomial kernel W_n ∩ ker(St_n → E_n) of a commutative ring is central and generated by symbols (Milnor Corollary 9.3, Theorem 9.11). The integer upper bound for K₂(ℤ) rests on it, and the T.3 part had requested it from T.2:symbols. This packet plans it there in seven nodes read from Milnor §9: the monomial subgroup with Lemma 9.1, conjugation by it, the finite-rank symbol, the generation theorem, the upper unipotent normal form, the T·W·T cover for fields, and the theorem that for a field the whole Steinberg kernel is monomial. The last gives K₂ of a field generated by symbols and K₂(𝔽_q) = 1 without Matsumoto's theorem, closing the finite-field gaps of the T.1 part. Verified routed rows attach the nodes to the accepted parts, narrow the stage citation of KTheoryLowDegrees U.4 to its accepted nodes, and answer the consumer requests made of T.5. The EllipticKTheory request for function-field tame kernels is routed back to its consumer, because its inputs lie downstream of T.5.

nodes.title: The monomial subgroup W_n(A) of the Steinberg group and its kernel C_n(A)
nodes.statement: Let A be a commutative ring and n ≥ 3, let St_n(A) be the finite-rank Steinberg group of T.1/steinberg-group-finite-rank and φ_n : St_n(A) → E_n(A) ⊆ GL_n(A) its elementary map (T.1:classical/to-elementary). The monomial subgroup W_n(A) ⊆ St_n(A) is the subgroup generated by the Weyl lift words w_ij(u) = x_ij(u) x_ji(−u⁻¹) x_ij(u), for i ≠ j and u ∈ A^× (T.2:symbols/diagonal-lift-words). It contains every diagonal lift h_ij(u) = w_ij(u) w_ij(−1) (T.2:symbols/diagonal-lift). The monomial kernel is C_n(A) = W_n(A) ∩ ker φ_n. Its image is described by Milnor's Lemma 9.1: φ_n(W_n(A)) is exactly the group of monomial matrices of determinant one, the matrices P_π·diag(v_1, …, v_n) with π a permutation, P_π e_k = e_{π(k)}, every v_k ∈ A^× and sign(π)·v_1⋯v_n = 1.
hypotheses: A is a commutative ring: the determinant condition and the diagonal-lift calculus use commutativity.
n ≥ 3, the range in which T.1 defines St_n(A); i, j are distinct indices in {1, …, n} and u ranges over A^×.
proofSteps: Define W_n(A) as the subgroup closure (mathlib:Subgroup.closure) of the set of all w_ij(u), and C_n(A) as its intersection with the kernel of φ_n. Each h_ij(u) is the product of the generators w_ij(u) and w_ij(−1), so it lies in W_n(A).

φ_n(w_ij(u)) has u in position (i, j), −u⁻¹ in position (j, i), 1 in the other diagonal positions and 0 elsewhere (T.2:symbols/diagonal-lift-words). Its 2 × 2 block [[0, u], [−u⁻¹, 0]] has determinant 1, so it is a monomial matrix of determinant one. φ_n(h_ij(u)) is diagonal, with u at i and u⁻¹ at j (T.2:symbols/diagonal-lift).

Lemma 9.1: these matrices generate every monomial matrix of determinant one. Write g = P_π D. A product of signed transpositions φ_n(w_ij(1)) equals P_π times a diagonal matrix of signs. The remaining diagonal factor has determinant one, so it is a product of the φ_n(h_1k(u_k)) = diag(u_k at 1, u_k⁻¹ at k), k = 2, …, n. On the matrix side, P_π D is tauceti:TauCeti.permutationGL π times tauceti:TauCeti.diagGL v. Mathlib's permutation matrix of σ sends e_j to e_{σ⁻¹(j)}, and Tau Ceti's permutationGL σ is the matrix of σ⁻¹, so P_π = permutationGL π. Its determinant is sign(π)·∏ v_k (mathlib:Matrix.det_permutation, tauceti:TauCeti.det_diagGL).

A ring map f : A → B sends w_ij(u) to w_ij(f(u)), hence W_n(A) into W_n(B) and C_n(A) into C_n(B). The stabilisation St_n(A) → St_{n+1}(A) of T.1/stabilisation sends generators to generators, hence W_n(A) into W_{n+1}(A) and C_n(A) into C_{n+1}(A).
For A = ℤ the units are ±1 and w_ij(−1) = w_ij(1)⁻¹ (weyl-conjugation (c)). So W_n(ℤ) is generated by the w_ij(1), and it is the monomial subgroup of T.5/integer-steinberg-word-model for n ≥ 3.
acceptance: Over ℤ with n = 3, φ_3(w_12(1)) is the signed transposition with rows (0, 1, 0), (−1, 0, 0), (0, 0, 1), of determinant one.
Over a field with q elements, φ_n(W_n) has n!·(q − 1)^(n−1) elements.
W_n(ℤ) agrees with the integer word model's monomial subgroup for n ≥ 3, and C_n(A) is the group of Milnor's Corollary 9.3 and Theorem 9.11.

nodes.title: Conjugation by the monomial subgroup permutes the root generators (Milnor 9.2–9.5)
nodes.statement: Let A be commutative and n ≥ 3. For w ∈ W_n(A) write φ_n(w) = P_π·diag(v_1, …, v_n) (monomial-subgroup). For i ≠ j, λ ∈ A and u ∈ A^×: (a) w x_ij(λ) w⁻¹ = x_{π(i)π(j)}(v_i λ v_j⁻¹); (b) w w_ij(u) w⁻¹ = w_{π(i)π(j)}(v_i u v_j⁻¹) and w h_ij(u) w⁻¹ = h_{π(i)π(j)}(v_i u v_j⁻¹)·h_{π(i)π(j)}(v_i v_j⁻¹)⁻¹; (c) w_ij(u)⁻¹ = w_ij(−u) and w_ij(u) = w_ji(−u⁻¹); (d) the subgroup H_n(A) generated by the h_ij(u) is normal in W_n(A); (e) C_n(A) lies in the centre of St_n(A). These are Milnor's Lemma 9.2, Corollaries 9.3 and 9.4 and Lemma 9.5.
hypotheses: A is commutative and n ≥ 3; i ≠ j, λ ∈ A, u ∈ A^×.
P_π e_k = e_{π(k)} and φ_n(w) = P_π D with D = diag(v_1, …, v_n); this factorisation exists by monomial-subgroup.
proofSteps: Lemma 9.2: conjugation by one generator w_kl(u) carries each x_ij(λ) to a single root generator. Split into Milnor's seven cases, according to which of i, j equal k or l. Each case is a calculation with the Steinberg relations in St_n(A) (T.1/steinberg-group-finite-rank). For example, if i = k and j ∉ {k, l} then w_kl(u) x_kj(λ) w_kl(u)⁻¹ = x_lj(−u⁻¹λ). If (i, j) = (k, l) then w_ij(u) x_ij(λ) w_ij(u)⁻¹ = x_ji(−u⁻²λ); T.2:symbols/field-proof/root-word-normalization records this case for fields. A general w is a word in the generators, and the statement follows by induction along the word.

Corollary 9.4: by step 1 the conjugate is some root generator x_ab(μ); apply φ_n. On matrices, P_π D e_ij(λ) D⁻¹ P_π⁻¹ = e_{π(i)π(j)}(v_i λ v_j⁻¹) (tauceti:TauCeti.permutationGL_mul_diagGL_mul_inv relabels the diagonal). A transvection with λ ≠ 0 determines its index pair and its parameter (tauceti:TauCeti.transvectionUnit, which is injective in the parameter), so (a, b, μ) = (π(i), π(j), v_i λ v_j⁻¹); the case λ = 0 is trivial. Multiplying out the defining words of w_ij and h_ij gives (b).

(c), Lemma 9.5: w_ij(u) w_ij(−u) = 1 follows from x_ij(a) x_ij(b) = x_ij(a + b) by cancelling the middle factors. Apply (b) to w = w_ij(u) itself: its permutation is the transposition (i j), with v_i = −u⁻¹ and v_j = u, so w_ij(u) = w w_ij(u) w⁻¹ = w_ji(v_i u v_j⁻¹) = w_ji(−u⁻¹).
(d): by the formula for h in (b), every conjugate of a generator h_ij(u) by an element of W_n(A) is a product of generators of H_n(A).
(e), Corollary 9.3: if φ_n(w) = 1 then π = 1 and every v_k = 1, so by (a) w commutes with every generator x_ij(λ). Hence w lies in the centre of St_n(A) (mathlib:Subgroup.center).
acceptance: w_12(1)⁴ = h_12(−1)⁻² lies in C_n(ℤ), so it is central in St_n(ℤ).
Over a field, the same-root and opposite-root cases agree with T.2:symbols/field-proof/root-word-normalization.

nodes.title: The finite-rank Steinberg symbol {u, v}_n in C_n(A)
nodes.statement: Let A be commutative and n ≥ 3. For u, v ∈ A^× and pairwise distinct indices i, j, k put {u, v}_n = [h_ij(u), h_ik(v)] = h_ij(u) h_ik(v) h_ij(u)⁻¹ h_ik(v)⁻¹ ∈ St_n(A). Then: (a) {u, v}_n = h_ik(uv) h_ik(u)⁻¹ h_ik(v)⁻¹ (Lemma 9.6); (b) {u, v}_n ∈ C_n(A), so it is central; (c) it does not depend on the triple (i, j, k); (d) it is bimultiplicative and skew-symmetric, {v, u}_n = ({u, v}_n)⁻¹ (Lemma 9.7); (e) {u, 1 − u}_n = 1 when u and 1 − u are units, and {u, −u}_n = 1 (Lemma 9.8); (f) stabilisation sends {u, v}_n to {u, v}_{n+1}, and its image in the stable group St(A) is the Steinberg symbol {u, v} of T.2/steinberg-symbol; (g) a ring map f sends {u, v}_n to {f(u), f(v)}_n. Milnor calls this the sharper, finite-rank meaning of the symbol.
hypotheses: A is commutative and n ≥ 3; u, v ∈ A^×; i, j, k pairwise distinct.
Commutators are [a, b] = aba⁻¹b⁻¹, the convention of T.2/steinberg-symbol and of T.2:symbols/field-proof/root-word-normalization.
proofSteps: (a): apply weyl-conjugation (b) to w = h_ij(u). Its image is diagonal with v_i = u, v_j = u⁻¹ and v_k = 1, so h_ij(u) h_ik(v) h_ij(u)⁻¹ = h_ik(uv) h_ik(u)⁻¹. Multiply on the right by h_ik(v)⁻¹.
(b): φ_n(h_ij(u)) and φ_n(h_ik(v)) are diagonal, so they commute and the commutator lies in W_n(A) ∩ ker φ_n = C_n(A). It is central by weyl-conjugation (e).

(d), bimultiplicativity for a fixed triple: by (a) at the triple (i, k, j), h_ij(uu′) = c·h_ij(u′)h_ij(u) with c = [h_ik(u), h_ij(u′)] central. The commutator identity [xy, z] = x[y, z]x⁻¹[x, z] and centrality then give {uu′, v}_n = {u, v}_n {u′, v}_n. The second variable is symmetric (Milnor Lemmas 8.1–8.2 and 9.7).

(c) and skew-symmetry: conjugate by an element w of W_n(A) whose permutation carries (i, j, k) to another triple and whose diagonal entries ε at those indices are ±1. By weyl-conjugation (b), h_ab(u) becomes h(εu)h(ε)⁻¹ at the new indices. By bimultiplicativity at the new triple the sign factors cancel in the commutator, and the conjugate of a central element is itself. Swapping j and k gives {v, u}_n = ({u, v}_n)⁻¹.

(e), Lemma 9.8: for v = 1 − u, show h_12(u) h_12(v) = h_12(uv) by rewriting w_12(u) w_12(−1) w_12(v) = w_12(uv) through w_12(−1) = w_21(1) = x_21(1) x_12(−1) x_21(1) and the conjugation formulas; this is the computation of T.2/steinberg-identity, carried out in St_3(A) ⊆ St_n(A). The hypothesis is symmetric in (u, v), so also h_12(v) h_12(u) = h_12(vu); since uv = vu these h's commute, and (a) gives {u, v}_n = 1. For v = −u, w_12(u) w_12(−1) w_12(−u) = w_12(u) w_12(−1) w_12(u)⁻¹ = w_12(−u²) by weyl-conjugation (b), (c), and the same argument applies.

(f): the stabilisation map of T.1/stabilisation sends x_ij(λ) to x_ij(λ), hence w, h and commutators to the same words. T.2/steinberg-symbol defines the stable symbol as this commutator in St(A). (g) is the same remark for a ring map.
acceptance: Over ℤ, {−1, −1}_3 = h_13(−1)⁻² = w_12(1)⁴ = (x_12 x_21(−1) x_12)⁴, the generator of Milnor's Theorem 10.1.
φ_n({u, v}_n) = 1 for all u, v.
The stable image is T.2's Steinberg symbol, so finite-rank and stable statements match.

nodes.title: Steinberg's theorem: the monomial kernel C_n(A) is generated by symbols (Milnor 9.11)
nodes.statement: Let A be a commutative ring and n ≥ 3. The monomial kernel C_n(A) = W_n(A) ∩ ker φ_n is the subgroup generated by the finite-rank symbols {u, v}_n, u, v ∈ A^× (Milnor's Theorem 9.11, due to Steinberg). In particular C_n(A) is abelian and central in St_n(A), and the description is compatible with stabilisation and with ring maps. For A = ℤ, C_n(ℤ) is generated by {−1, −1}_n = w_12(1)⁴ and has at most two elements.
hypotheses: The theorem concerns W_n(A) ∩ ker φ_n only. That the whole kernel of φ_n lies in W_n is a separate statement: field-kernel-is-monomial proves it for fields, and T.5/integer-kernel-in-monomial-subgroup for ℤ.
proofSteps: Let H = H_n(A) ⊆ W_n(A) be the subgroup generated by the h_ij(u); it is normal in W_n(A) (weyl-conjugation (d)).

C_n(A) ⊆ H. Modulo H, w_ij(u) ≡ w_ij(1), since w_ij(u) w_ij(1)⁻¹ = w_ij(u) w_ij(−1) = h_ij(u). Write w̄_ij for the common class; w̄_ij = w̄_ji by weyl-conjugation (c), and w̄_ij² = 1 since w_ij(1)² = h_ij(−1)⁻¹. By weyl-conjugation (b), w̄_ij w̄_kl ≡ w̄_{τ(k)τ(l)} w̄_ij with τ the transposition (i j). Take c ∈ C_n(A) as a word in the w_ij(u). Push every w̄_1l to the left past the w̄_ij with i, j > 1 (these fix the index 1). Then cancel w̄_1l w̄_1l ≡ 1 and rewrite w̄_1j w̄_1l ≡ w̄_1l w̄_lj for j ≠ l, removing the w̄_1l one or two at a time, until at most one remains on the left. A single remaining w̄_1l is impossible, because the permutation part of φ_n(c) is the identity and the rest of the word fixes 1. Repeat with the index 2, and so on, to get c ≡ 1 modulo H (Milnor's word reduction).

Lemma 9.10: h_jk(u) = h_ik(u) h_ij(u)⁻¹ for pairwise distinct i, j, k. This comes from evaluating the commutator h_ik(u) w_jk(1) h_ik(u)⁻¹ w_jk(1)⁻¹ in two ways with weyl-conjugation (b). Hence h_jk(u) h_kj(u) = 1, and H is generated by the h_1k(u), k = 2, …, n.

Let C* ⊆ C_n(A) be the subgroup generated by the symbols; it is central (finite-rank-symbol (b)), hence normal. Modulo C*, h_1l(uv) ≡ h_1l(u) h_1l(v) by finite-rank-symbol (a) at a triple (1, j, l), j ∉ {1, l}, which needs n ≥ 3. Also h_1j(u) h_1l(v) ≡ h_1l(v) h_1j(u), by finite-rank-symbol (a)–(c) when j ≠ l and by commutativity of A when j = l. So c ≡ h_12(u_2) h_13(u_3) ⋯ h_1n(u_n) modulo C*.
Apply φ_n: φ_n(c) = diag(u_2⋯u_n, u_2⁻¹, …, u_n⁻¹) (tauceti:TauCeti.diagGL). Since φ_n(c) = 1, every u_k = 1, so c ∈ C*. The reverse inclusion C* ⊆ C_n(A) is finite-rank-symbol (b).
Stabilisation and ring maps send C_n to C_n and symbols to symbols (monomial-subgroup, finite-rank-symbol (f), (g)), so the description is compatible with both.

A = ℤ: the units are ±1 and symbols with an entry 1 are trivial, so C_n(ℤ) is generated by {−1, −1}_n. Moreover ({−1, −1}_n)² = {1, −1}_n = 1 by bimultiplicativity, and {−1, −1}_n = w_12(1)⁴ by finite-rank-symbol.
acceptance: Over ℤ, C_3(ℤ) ⊆ {1, w_12(1)⁴}. With T.5/integer-kernel-in-monomial-subgroup this bounds K₂(ℤ), which is its use in T.5/integer-kernel-upper-generation.
Over a finite field, together with finite-rank-symbol (d), (e) and the cyclic-annihilator argument (T.2:symbols/field-proof/cyclic-annihilator), C_n(𝔽_q) = 1: Milnor's Corollary 9.9.
The reduction modulo H uses only the permutation part of φ_n: W_n(A)/H_n(A) maps onto the symmetric group, and the word reduction shows that this map has trivial kernel.

nodes.title: The upper unipotent subgroup T_n(A) maps isomorphically onto U_n(A) (Milnor 9.14)
nodes.statement: Let A be a commutative ring and n ≥ 3, and let T_n(A) ⊆ St_n(A) be the subgroup generated by the x_ij(λ) with i < j. Every element of T_n(A) is a product ∏_{i<j} x_ij(λ_ij), with the factors in lexicographic order of (i, j) and uniquely determined λ_ij ∈ A. Consequently φ_n restricts to an isomorphism of T_n(A) onto the upper unitriangular group U_n(A) (Tau Ceti's upperUnitriangularGroup). Moreover, for each i < n the subgroup T′_i generated by the x_kl(μ), k < l, (k, l) ≠ (i, i + 1), is normal in T_n(A), and T_n(A) = x_{i,i+1}(A)·T′_i.
hypotheses: A is commutative and n ≥ 3; the order on pairs (i, j), i < j, is lexicographic.
proofSteps: Existence of the ordered form: induct on the height l − k, collecting factors with the Steinberg relations of St_n(A) (T.1/steinberg-group-finite-rank). These are [x_ij(λ), x_jl(μ)] = x_il(λμ) for distinct i, j, l, and commutation for non-chaining pairs. A commutator of two positive-root generators involves only a root of larger height, so the collection terminates.

Uniqueness: put R_i = ∏_{j>i} x_ij(λ_ij). The factors of R_i commute, and φ_n(R_i) = I + Σ_{j>i} λ_ij E_ij changes only row i. Write M = φ_n(R_1⋯R_{n−1}) and N_{i+1} = φ_n(R_{i+1}⋯R_{n−1}). Row i of M equals e_i + Σ_{j>i} λ_ij·(row j of N_{i+1}), and the rows j > i of N_{i+1} form an invertible unitriangular block. So the λ_ij are recovered from M row by row, from the last row up.

The same triangular system shows that every upper unitriangular matrix is such a product, so φ_n maps T_n(A) bijectively onto U_n(A) (tauceti:TauCeti.upperUnitriangularGroup; tauceti:TauCeti.UpperUnitriangularGroup.ext determines its elements by their entries above the diagonal). The matrix-side relations are tauceti:TauCeti.commutatorElement_transvectionUnit and tauceti:TauCeti.commute_transvectionUnit.

Normality of T′_i: the commutator of x_{i,i+1}(λ) with x_kl(μ), (k, l) ≠ (i, i + 1), is trivial, or equals x_il(λμ) when k = i + 1, or x_{k,i+1}(−μλ) when l = i. Each of these lies in T′_i, so T_n(A) = x_{i,i+1}(A)·T′_i.
acceptance: For n = 3, x_12(a) x_13(b) x_23(c) maps to the matrix with rows (1, a, b + ac), (0, 1, c), (0, 0, 1). Its entries recover a and c, and then b.
This is injectivity of φ_n on the upper unipotent subgroup only, not on St_n(A); field-kernel-is-monomial uses it for t₂ = t₁⁻¹.
The complement T′_i of the simple root (i, i + 1) is the subgroup whose generators are permuted, among positive roots, by conjugation with w_{i,i+1}(1) (weyl-conjugation (a)).

nodes.title: For a field, St_n(F) = T·W·T (Milnor 9.15)
nodes.statement: Let F be a field and n ≥ 3. Every element of St_n(F) lies in T_n(F)·W_n(F)·T_n(F), where T_n(F) is the upper unipotent subgroup of upper-unipotent-normal-form and W_n(F) the monomial subgroup.
hypotheses: F is a commutative field and n ≥ 3. Milnor states the lemma for skew fields as well; the atlas uses fields only.
proofSteps: St_n(F) is generated by T_n(F) and the w_{i,i+1}(1), i < n. The x_ij(λ) with |i − j| = 1 generate St_n(F) by the commutator relations, and w_ij(1) x_ij(λ) w_ij(1)⁻¹ = x_ji(−λ) (weyl-conjugation (a)) turns each lower one into a conjugate of an upper one.

So it suffices that T W T is closed under right multiplication by w = w_{i,i+1}(1). Given t₁ w′ t₂, write t₂ = x_{i,i+1}(λ) t′ with t′ ∈ T′_i (upper-unipotent-normal-form). Then t₁ w′ t₂ w = t₁ (w′ x_{i,i+1}(λ) w)(w⁻¹ t′ w), and w⁻¹ t′ w ∈ T_n(F): conjugation by w_{i,i+1}(1)⁻¹ = w_{i,i+1}(−1) permutes the positive roots other than (i, i + 1) (weyl-conjugation (a), (c)).
Let π be the permutation of φ_n(w′). Case 1, π(i) < π(i + 1): w′ x_{i,i+1}(λ) w = x_{π(i)π(i+1)}(λ′) w′ w ∈ T W.

Case 2, π(i) > π(i + 1) and λ ≠ 0. Write x_{i,i+1}(λ) = w_{i,i+1}(λ) x_{i,i+1}(−λ) x_{i+1,i}(λ⁻¹), so w′ x_{i,i+1}(λ) w = (w′ w_{i,i+1}(λ) x_{i,i+1}(−λ))(x_{i+1,i}(λ⁻¹) w). The permutation of w′ w_{i,i+1}(λ) sends (i, i + 1) to (π(i + 1), π(i)), a positive root, so the first factor lies in T W. The second is w x_{i,i+1}(−λ⁻¹) ∈ W T, by conjugation with w_{i,i+1}(−1).

Case 3, λ = 0: the factor is w′ w ∈ W. Every nonzero λ is a unit because F is a field; over a ring, a nonzero non-unit parameter falls outside cases 2 and 3, and this is where the field hypothesis is used.
acceptance: The matrix shadow is the Bruhat decomposition SL_n(F) = ⋃ U·N·U, and the upper-triangular monomial matrices are diagonal (tauceti:TauCeti.UpperTriangularGroup.mem_diagonalTorus_of_mem, over fields with a unit other than 1).
For n = 3 and F = 𝔽₂, every element of St_3(𝔽₂) is t₁ w t₂ with t₁, t₂ upper unipotent and w in the group generated by the w_ij(1).
Only cases 1–3 occur, and case 2 needs λ invertible: the lemma is stated for fields.

nodes.title: For a field, the whole Steinberg kernel is monomial and generated by symbols (Milnor 9.12)
nodes.statement: Let F be a field and n ≥ 3. The kernel of φ_n : St_n(F) → E_n(F) is contained in W_n(F), hence equals C_n(F). So it is central in St_n(F) and is generated by the finite-rank symbols {u, v}_n (generated-by-symbols): St_n(F) → E_n(F) is a central extension whose kernel is generated by symbols, for every n ≥ 3. Passing to the colimit, K₂(F) is generated by the stable Steinberg symbols {u, v} (Milnor's Theorem 9.12 and Corollary 9.13); this is the field clause of T.2/symbols-generate.
hypotheses: F is a commutative field and n ≥ 3.

For skew fields Milnor proves the containment of the kernel in W_n but not generation by symbols, which needs commutativity (generated-by-symbols). The atlas states the field case; see the source issue K2SymbolsBrauer/E-T5-division-ring-attribution.
proofSteps: Write x ∈ ker φ_n as t₁ w t₂ with t₁, t₂ ∈ T_n(F) and w ∈ W_n(F) (field-bruhat-cover).

Then φ_n(w) = φ_n(t₁)⁻¹ φ_n(t₂)⁻¹ is a monomial matrix that is upper unitriangular. A monomial matrix P_π D that is upper triangular has π = 1: column j has its single nonzero entry v_j in row π(j) ≤ j, and the only such permutation is the identity. Unitriangularity then forces D = 1. Tau Ceti's tauceti:TauCeti.UpperTriangularGroup.mem_diagonalTorus_of_mem gives this argument for the diagonal normalizer over fields with a unit other than 1; it holds over every nonzero commutative ring.
Hence φ_n(w) = 1, so w ∈ C_n(F); and φ_n(t₂) = φ_n(t₁)⁻¹, so t₂ = t₁⁻¹ because φ_n is injective on T_n(F) (upper-unipotent-normal-form).
Therefore x = t₁ w t₁⁻¹ = w, since w is central (weyl-conjugation (e)). So ker φ_n ⊆ W_n(F), equality with C_n(F) holds by definition, and generation by symbols is generated-by-symbols.

Stable consequence: an element of K₂(F) = ker(St(F) → E(F)) comes from some St_n(F), n ≥ 3 (T.1/stabilisation), with trivial image in E_n(F) since E_n(F) → E(F) is injective. So it is a product of finite-rank symbols, whose stable images are the Steinberg symbols {u, v} (finite-rank-symbol (f)).
acceptance: For F = 𝔽_q every finite-rank symbol is 1, by finite-rank-symbol (d), (e) and the cyclic-annihilator argument. So St_n(𝔽_q) → E_n(𝔽_q) is an isomorphism for n ≥ 3, and K₂(𝔽_q) = 1 (Milnor Corollaries 9.9 and 9.13), with no appeal to Matsumoto's theorem.
For F = ℝ the kernel is nontrivial: {−1, −1}_3 is a nontrivial central element of St_3(ℝ), detected after stabilisation by the real sign symbol.
Its stable consequence is the field clause of T.2/symbols-generate (routed row R3 of restructure).

sourceIssues.correction: Milnor §9 proves generation by symbols for fields only. Theorem 9.11 (C_n generated by the symbols {u, v}) assumes the ring commutative, and Corollary 9.13 states the conclusion for fields. For skew fields §9 proves only that the Steinberg kernel lies in the monomial subgroup W and equals C_n (Theorem 9.12). sourceIssues.reason: Milnor states Theorem 9.11 for an arbitrary commutative ring (p. 76). Its proof needs h_1l(uv) ≡ h_1l(u)h_1l(v) modulo symbols, which is the bimultiplicativity of Lemma 9.7, also stated only for commutative rings. Corollary 9.13 (p. 78) draws the generation conclusion for fields. Theorem 9.12 is the only statement of the section that covers skew fields, and its conclusion is the containment of the kernel in W.
